faq.q_beginner: Can I join if I'm a beginner?
faq.a_beginner: Absolutely! We have beginner friendly guided projects and weekly calls where you can ask for help!
faq.a_teams: Yes! After creating a new project, you can invite your teammates!
faq.a_eligible: You must be a teenager (ages 13-18), and under 19 before August 2026.
faq.a_cant_come: We will have an online shop where you can purchase prizes such as 3D printers, tools, and more!
faq.a_free: Yes! Each of your projects will be funded, and the event itself is 100% free. We also have need-based flight stipends available.
faq.a_hackclub: Hack Club is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit (EIN: 81-2908499) that helps high school students learn to code and build projects. We're the largest teen-led coding community, with over 50,000 students building projects with their friends each year.
faq.a_bogota: Bogotá is the capital of Colombia and a hub for tech businesses across South America. It's vibrant, creative, and full of incredible energy, which makes it the perfect place to bring teenagers together from around the world to hack, explore, and build.
faq.a_more: Ask us in #macondo on the Hack Club Slack, or email us at macondo{'@'}hackclub.com!

project_streaks.heading: Project streaks
project_streaks.freeze_rule: If you don't work on any of your projects on a given day, one streak freeze gets used to keep your streaks alive. When you run out of freezes, every project's streak resets to 0.
project_streaks.auto_use_description: Turns auto-freeze on or off for every project at once. Projects with it on are protected: working an hour on any project keeps them alive, and freezes cover fully missed days. A project with it off resets to 0 on the first day without an hour on that specific project. A dash means some projects are on and some are off.

currency_page.heading: How currency works
currency_page.intro: You earn gold while building and spend it in the shop. Streaks multiply the gold you get when you ship a project. Fruits live on as a historical badge of what you've earned.
currency_page.gold_blurb: The spendable currency. Buy things in the shop.
currency_page.fruits_blurb: A historical record of what each ship would have earned in fruit. Counted on this page, not spent.
currency_page.streaks_blurb: Show up daily to earn a gold multiplier on every ship.
currency_page.starfruit_blurb: Awarded for extra-fruity ships. Spend to unlock a locked shop item.
currency_page.lifetime_fruits_blurb: Fruit you've earned over your lifetime, automatically converted to gold at ship-approval time. Pure history, no balance to spend.
currency_page.lifetime_fruits_footnote: Includes everything earned before the gold-only switch, plus every ship since.
currency_page.tier_chart_description: Each project is assigned a fruit based on its type (software or hardware) and complexity level. The fruit determines the project's gold-per-hour rate.
currency_page.level_1_description: Starter projects. LEDs, simple circuits, first websites.
currency_page.level_2_description: Real builds. Macropads, custom designs, small apps.
currency_page.level_3_description: Complex systems. Robots, wearables, custom firmware.
currency_page.level_4_description: Ambitious work. Autonomous robots, FPGAs, satellites.
currency_page.converter_description: Estimate the gold value of a ship at a given project streak. Type the base fruit reward (before any streak), and the panel walks through the same math the server runs at ship approval: base fruit × project streak, then each fruit converts to gold at the flat shop rate. The streak only multiplies the fruit you earn at ship time, converting fruit to gold later never applies a bonus.
currency_page.converter_step_gold_hint: Floored per fruit type, like the convert endpoint
currency_page.streak_description: Every day you work on a project, that project's streak ticks up by one. When you ship, the project's streak multiplies the gold reward by 1 + (streak × 0.01), so a 30-day streak earns you 1.30x as much gold. Miss a day and the streak resets, so streak freezes from the shop are worth it.
currency_page.streak_per_project_note: Each project tracks its own streak. The slider is just an example, your real streak depends on the project you're shipping.
currency_page.streak_footnote: Multiplier is snapshotted at ship time. Long streaks before shipping are worth the wait.
currency_page.calc_description: Plug in a project's type, level, hours, and current streak to see the gold a ship would award. It uses the same per-hour rates, fruit assignment, and plant-stage tiers the platform pays out.
currency_page.calc_formula_empty: Enter hours and a streak to calculate

tutorial_challenges.delete_src: Delete the src="..." part from the <img> tag. What happens to the image?

tutorial_challenges.free_form_change_text: Try changing the text inside the <p> tag, or edit the <h1> to say something different.
tutorial_challenges.free_form_image: Now find an image online. Right-click it, copy the image address, and add it back to the <img> tag, like: <img src="https://example.com/cat.jpg" alt="A cute cat" />

tutorial_challenges.free_form_tailwind_color_more: Try adding a color to the paragraph (like text-gray-700), or make the image round with rounded-full.

html_structure.title: HTML Structure
html_structure.goal_description: By the end of this tutorial you'll have built your own site like this: a personal page you can actually share with your friends and family. Every webpage is made of HTML and CSS, and you'll shape each piece of yours yourself as we go.
html_structure.explain_content:
When you deleted the <p> line, the text vanished from the preview. Everything inside <body> is what the visitor sees. Remove the content, and there's nothing to show.

When you typed it back with different text, the preview updated instantly. The browser reads your HTML and displays whatever it finds inside the <body>.

HTML pages are made up of tags like these:

  • <!DOCTYPE html>: tells the browser "this is an HTML5 document"
  • <html>: the root element that wraps everything
  • <head>: the part of the page that holds info ABOUT the site, not stuff people see. The page title, the language, and links to stylesheets all go here. Think of it as the settings area the browser reads before drawing anything.
  • <body>: everything the visitor actually sees on the page
  • <h1>: a heading, the biggest, boldest text on the page
  • <p>: a paragraph of regular text
  • <img>: an image that uses a src attribute to point to a picture
html_structure.apply_instructions: On the empty line after </head>, add <body> and </body>. Then inside the body (between <body> and </body>), add a paragraph like: <p>Hello world!</p>

add_content.title: Add Content
add_content.goal_description: Headings make text bigger and bolder. Here's a page showing different heading sizes alongside regular paragraph text.
add_content.explain_content:
When you changed <h1> to <h5>, the heading got much smaller. HTML has six heading levels; the number tells the browser how important the heading is:

<h1>: Biggest
<h2>: Second
<h3>: Medium
<h4>: Smaller
<h5>: Even smaller
<h6>: Smallest

The <p> tag creates paragraphs of text. You can have as many as you want, and each one starts on a new line.

Every tag that wraps text needs both an opening tag (like <h1>) and a closing tag (like </h1>).
add_content.apply_instructions: Add an <h1> with your name inside <body>, like: <h1>Your Name</h1>. Then add a <p> about yourself below it.

add_image.title: Add an Image
add_image.goal_description: Images live in an <img> tag. It's self-closing (no </img>) and needs two things: src (the URL) and alt (a short description).
add_image.explain_content:
When you deleted the src attribute, the image disappeared; the browser had no address to fetch. But the alt text showed up in its place, letting visitors know what was supposed to be there.

When you added a new URL, the image came back. The src is the address of the image file, and alt is the backup description.

How the <img> tag works

  • src: the URL (address) of the image file
  • alt: text shown if the image can't load, and read by screen readers for accessibility
  • <img> is self-closing: it doesn't wrap around content like <p>...</p>
add_image.apply_instructions: Add an <img src="..." /> tag between <body> and </body>. Use a real image URL. Right-click any image online and copy its address.

add_tailwind.title: Add Tailwind
add_tailwind.goal_description: HTML sets what's on the page. CSS sets how it looks, but it's a whole separate language. Normally you'd write rules in their own file, like h1 { color: blue; }, then link that file to your HTML so the browser knows which rules go with which tags. That's a lot more moving parts than we can fit here, so we're going to skip CSS for now (MDN's CSS guide is a great place to learn it properly later). Instead we'll use Tailwind: a one-line script that lets you style elements by dropping ready-made labels like class="text-blue-500" straight on the tag, no separate rules needed.
add_tailwind.explain_content:
The <script> tag

The <script src="https://cdn.tailwindcss.com"> line loads the Tailwind Play CDN, a small JavaScript library. Once loaded, it watches your HTML for class names and generates the matching CSS on the fly, so styles show up instantly without you writing a stylesheet.

What Tailwind replaces

Normally, to style an element you'd create a style.css file, link it with <link>, and write rules like h1 { color: blue; }. Tailwind replaces all of that. Each class is a pre-made rule, and you apply it directly on the element with class="...". No separate file, no <link>, no selectors.

The class you just used

  • text-blue-500 is color: #3b82f6;: that's the blue you see on the heading.

You'll stack a few more of these in the next step.
add_tailwind.apply_instructions: Inside <head>, add <script src="https://cdn.tailwindcss.com"></script>. Then give one of your elements a Tailwind class, like class="text-blue-500" on the <h1>.

style_with_tailwind.title: Style with Tailwind
style_with_tailwind.goal_description: Stack multiple Tailwind labels in one class="...", separated by spaces, to style an element several ways at once. Here's what a styled version looks like.
style_with_tailwind.explain_content:
You stacked two Tailwind classes on the <body> at once. Each class is a standalone shortcut for a single CSS rule, and Tailwind merges them without conflict: class="text-center bg-pink-100" gives you centered text AND a pink background, with no stylesheet in sight.

The classes you just used

  • text-center is text-align: center;
  • bg-pink-100 is background-color: #fce7f3;

A few more to try

A short reference of classes in the same three families (background, text color, text style). The size ramp goes sm → base → lg and keeps going up through xl, 2xl, all the way to 9xl.

  • text-sm / text-base / text-lg: small, default, large text
  • text-left / text-center / text-right: text alignment
  • font-bold: bold text
  • italic: italic text
  • underline: underlined text
  • uppercase: ALL CAPS text
  • text-blue-500 / text-gray-800: text color (pick any color + shade)
  • bg-pink-100 / bg-gray-900: background color (same idea)

When you want more classes, add them to the same class="" with spaces in between. Try a few of these on your own site in the next phase.
style_with_tailwind.apply_instructions: This is your site. Add Tailwind classes to at least two different elements. Mix and match anything from the reference: text sizes, alignment, text colors, background colors, font weights. The goal is to make the page look the way you want. Full reference: tailwindcss.com docs.

readme.title: Write a README
readme.goal_description: A README is a short file that tells people what your project is. It's written in Markdown, a plain-text format with a couple of simple symbols for formatting.
readme.explain_content:
Markdown is just plain text with a few symbols that the renderer turns into formatting. Here are the ones you need:

  • # at the start of a line makes a big heading. ## is smaller, ### smaller still.
  • **bold** wraps text in asterisks to make it bold.
  • - item at the start of a line makes a bullet point.
  • Blank lines separate paragraphs.

That's the whole syntax you need for a first README. Next up, write one for your site.
readme.apply_instructions: Write a short README for your site. Include a # heading on the first line, then a sentence or two below it. A bullet list with - is optional. Click Next when you're done.

project.entry_title: Here, tap this patch of soil.
project.entry_body: That's where your project will grow. Give it a click.
project.step1_body: Put in a description of something you want to build, then hit Continue.
project.step2_body: Pick something short. You can rename it later. Hit Continue when you're happy with it.
project.step3_body: Pick whichever fits. If you're not sure, software is a safe bet. Hit Continue when you've chosen.
project.step4_body: Pick one, then hit Create Project to plant it. Beginner grows fast, Expert takes real work.
project.submit_body: Hit Create. I'll handle the rest.
project.landed_body: This is where you'll manage everything about your project. Let me show you around.
project.title_edit_title: Click the title to rename it.
project.title_edit_body: Hover over the title and a pencil shows up. Click it (or the title itself) to edit. Most fields on this page work the same way.
project.description_edit_title: The description works the same way.
project.description_edit_body: Click to edit. Markdown is supported: bold, lists, links, code. Keep it clear so reviewers know what you built.
project.thumbnail_body: Click the banner to upload an image. A screenshot or photo of your project makes a big difference when reviewers see it.
project.checklist_body: Every box needs a green check before you can submit. Repo URL, demo URL, thumbnail, and proof of work. Anything missing shows a red X.
project.journals_body: Write short updates with screenshots as you build. Hardware projects need at least one journal to ship. Software projects can use Hackatime hours, or both.
project.ship_body: Once every checklist box is green, this lights up. Hit it to submit for review and earn fruit. Reviewers usually respond within a few days.
project.finish_body: Work on your project, fill in the boxes, and ship it when you're ready. I'll be here on the farm if you need me.
